title: I've never been there
goal: Talk about experiences — what you have and haven't done — with the perfect tense, and face the fact that this form **follows the speaker's gender**.
bekal: forming the perfect with **съм** + the past participle
matching it to gender and number
telling the perfect apart from the aorist
asking about experiences with **бил ли си…?**

dialogs.title: Диалог — A trip to Plovdiv
dialogs.intro: Maria suggests a trip. Watch the ending of the verb in the perfect — it changes depending on who is speaking, a man or a woman.

notes: ⚠️ **The perfect follows the speaker's gender.** A woman says *била съм*, a man *бил съм*. A woman *не съм ходила*, a man *не съм ходил*. For several people: *били сме*, *ходили сме*. This is the biggest pitfall of the unit for English speakers, because English never marks gender on a verb. **If you are a woman, get used to saying -ла at the end.**

**When to use the perfect and when the aorist?** The perfect is used when what matters is **the result now**, not when it happened: *Бил съм в Пловдив* (I have been to Plovdiv — an experience I carry with me). The aorist is used when the event has a specific time: *Отидох в Пловдив миналата година* (I went to Plovdiv last year). ⚠️ If there is a clear time expression, use the aorist — just like English "I went", not "I have been", with "last year".

**Никога не съм ходила там — notice the negatives working together.** *Никога* requires *не*, and *не* stands before *съм*. This also explains why *съм* can come early here: what opens the sentence is *никога*, not *съм*.
**Той ходил ли е — watch where ли goes.** In the perfect, *ли* slips in after the participle and before *е*. It sounds odd at first but you get used to it quickly.
**Пет пъти means "five times".** The word *път* means "time" and also "road", and its masculine counting form is *пъти*: *един път, два пъти, много пъти*. For "the first time": *за първи път*.

**Пловдив really is older than Rome, and not by a little.** People were living there around six thousand years before Christ, making it the oldest continuously inhabited city in Europe — older than Athens and Rome. Its Roman theater is still used for concerts today.

**Обиколил comes from обикалям — "to go around".** The prefix **о-** marks movement around something. Prefixes like this change the meaning of Bulgarian verbs deeply and are one of the biggest topics of level A2.

**Стария град and римския театър use the short form** even though neither is an object. In everyday speech, the long/short rule is often ignored — something Unit 3 already warned about. In writing, the correct form is *Старият град*.

grammars.title: The perfect — съм + past participle
body: This form has two parts: the verb **съм**, which follows the subject, and the participle, which follows the **gender and number** of the subject.
after: The participle is formed from the *аз* past form by changing **-х** to **-л**: *работих* → *работил*, *четох* → *чел*, *видях* → *видял*, *бях* → *бил*.

⚠️ Some forms are irregular and must be memorized: *чел* (from чета), *ял* (from ям), *пил* (from пия), *дошъл / дошла / дошли* (from дойда), *отишъл / отишла / отишли* (from отида). Notice the **ъ** that appears in the masculine and disappears in the other forms — the same pattern as the adjective *топъл / топла* in Unit 12.

grammars.title: Perfect versus aorist — which one to choose
body: Both talk about the past, but they answer different questions.
after: A quick test that is almost always right, and works like English: **if your sentence could use "ever", "never" or "already", use the perfect. If it says exactly when, use the aorist.**
To ask about experiences, the standard form is: *Бил ли си в…?* (to a man), *Била ли си в…?* (to a woman), *Били ли сте в…?* (formal or plural).

blocks.text: You'll use *За първи път съм тук* a lot, and it almost always opens a long conversation. Bulgarians are very curious about what newcomers think of their country, and the next question is almost certain: *Харесва ли ти?* (Do you like it?)

sections.title: Five places people will tell you about

head: Place
Say it
Why
rows: The oldest continuously inhabited city in Europe. Its Old Town is hilly and cobbled, full of brightly painted nineteenth-century wooden houses, with a Roman theater still in use.
Former capital of the Second Bulgarian Empire, its houses piled up on cliffs above a bend of the river Янтра.
A monastery in the mountains with black-and-white striped pillars and frescoes covering every surface. Two hours from Sofia.
A small town on a rocky peninsula on the Black Sea, with dozens of medieval churches.
The Rose Valley near Казанлък, where most of the world's rose oil is produced. The harvest is in May, before sunrise.

blocks.text: Bulgarian rose oil — **розово масло** — is still a key ingredient in luxury perfumes worldwide, and one kilogram takes about three tons of petals. If you want a truly Bulgarian souvenir, this is it.

blocks.title: The alphabet that was born here
items: On May 24, all of Bulgaria celebrates **Ден на българската азбука, просвета и култура** — the day of the Bulgarian alphabet, education and culture. Schoolchildren march with flowers and big paper letters.

What is celebrated is not independence or a war victory, but an **alphabet**. Cyril and Methodius created the Glagolitic script in the ninth century; their students in Preslav, Bulgaria, developed the Cyrillic script you are learning now.
From here the script spread to Serbia, Russia, Ukraine, and eventually Mongolia. If you want to make a Bulgarian proud: *Кирилицата е родена тук, нали?* (Cyrillic was born here, right?)
